title: CampaignView, a database of policy platforms and biographical narratives for congressional candidates
coverage: Full text read in one pass (885 lines): abstract through references, all tables. No lobbying, network, path-finding or allocation content in paper. Elections, legislators and text measurement covered. Paul markup: none (annot_sha12s empty, no note flag). Page images not rendered. Corrections: full author names; venue, DOI, type filled; kind academic-article changed to data descriptor. Text gives 5,228 corpus candidates (abstract) vs 5,300 with a website (Methods p.4).
research_question: No hypothesis is tested. The paper asks how to supply systematic, real-time text of congressional candidate campaign websites (platforms and biographies) for 2018 to 2022 House primaries, so that questions on polarization, agenda-setting and representation can be studied (Abstract p.1; Background p.2).
theory: Not tested. Motivation cites candidate self-presentation and position-taking (refs 4-6), issue emphasis shaping voter perceptions and media attention (refs 7-9), campaign priorities predicting later legislative priorities (refs 10-12), and primaries as the pivotal competitive stage (refs 13-18), p.1-2.
data: Population: 6,016 major-party, ballot-eligible House primary candidates, 2018-2022. Corpus: 5,228 candidates (86.9%); 43,465 platform points (candidate-year-point); 5,114 biographies (candidate-year). Collection: manual scrape of campaign sites one week before each primary, plus Wayback Machine for 1,111 candidates (archived text is 7.8%). Auxiliary: party, incumbency, vote shares, FEC ID, BioGuideID, fundraising. Release: Harvard Dataverse doi 10.7910/DVN/JIEAPT (CC0).
method: Descriptive data construction. Name standardization by probabilistic record linkage on pretrained word embeddings, blocked on party and state; matches under 50% probability hand-checked (p.8-9). Every platform point hand-labeled into one of 14 Major Policy Topic codes by trained annotators with a codebook (p.3). Topic term lists from keyness analysis (Table 2, p.7). Missingness described by logistic regression of website, biography and platform absence on covariates (Table 5, p.9). Relabeling check on a 20% random sample (8,584 points) by other coders (p.10).
identification: None. Table 5 missingness coefficients are associations only. No causal design.
scope: U.S. House major-party, ballot-eligible primary candidates, 2018 to 2022 cycles. Population of campaign websites and platforms only, not all candidate communications. Era: 2018-2022 redistricting decade. Partisan dynamics are reported for platforms only (Fig. 3, p.10).
measures: Major Policy Topic code (14 categories, Table 1 examples, Table 6 crosswalk to PAP and CRS). Biography and platform presence flags. Platform subheadings. Primary and general vote shares. Party, incumbency, prior office holding (quality_cand). Logged fundraising. Primary type (Open, Partially-Closed, Non-Partisan). Unopposed primary flag. Presidential vote share by district (dem_prez_vote). Identifiers: FECCandID, BioGuideID, housegov_bio flag, housegov_issue flag.

key_findings.finding: Corpus covers 5,228 candidates, 86.9% of 6,016 eligible House primary candidates, 2018-2022; 43,465 platform points and 5,114 biographies.
Campaign website identified for 5,300 candidates (88.1%); 85.0% of those had a platform and 96.5% a biography.
Missingness: no biography for 14.99%, no platform for 25.08%, no website at all for 11.9% of the 6,016 candidates.
Archived Wayback data supplies 7.8% of candidates; 239 in 2018, 101 in 2020, 67 in 2022. 1,111 candidates (18.5%) had no primary-season data.
Unopposed primary is negatively associated with missing website, biography and platform (-0.342, -0.349, -0.320; all significant at 95%).

Current incumbent MC has the largest negative association with missing website (-2.967), biography (-2.000) and platform (-0.314). Logged fundraising is negative for all three (-0.222, -0.194, -0.136).
Three-quarters of candidates without a website raised under 100,000 dollars. Website-plus-platform present for 88.3% of general election winners and biography for 99.0%.
Hand-coding reliability on a 20% relabel (8,584 points): percent agreement 80%, Cohen kappa 0.84, weighted kappa 0.74. Most disagreements were on Unknown/Other.
Name linkage across cycles: 15 wrong matches for 2018-2020, 1 for 2020-2022, none for 2018-2022.
Democrats consistently emphasize Energy and Environment, Healthcare and Social Welfare; Republicans emphasize Immigration and Government Operations more often.
Education partisan gap about 25 points before 2022, narrowing to about 5 points in 2022. Healthcare gap 23 points in 2020 and over 40 points in 2022 (driven by fewer Republicans discussing it).
Platform text is cleaned and parsed to the policy level, so one row is one platform point (statement_id), aggregable to candidate-year.

limitations: About 12% of eligible candidates have no website and 25% have no platform, with missingness concentrated among uncompetitive and low-fundraising candidates. Each platform point gets one topic (majority content), so multi-topic issues such as women rights or reproductive health may be under-coded (p.10). Topic codes are only partly aligned to PAP and CRS schemes (Table 6). Reliability check covers only the 2022 relabel sample. Redistricting changes district IDs, so cd is not a recommended key. Website text is a snapshot one week before primary.

short_quotes: Our corpus covers 5,228 candidates, representing 86.9% of major-party, ballot-eligible contenders who ran for the U.S. House
Currently, there is no open-source database of text from congressional candidate campaign websites.
Percent agreement between re-labeled documents and their original topical coding was 80%.
